mainEntity.name: What makes an AIR unsound in practice?

acceptedAnswer.text: Under-constrained columns: a register nobody binds on non-flag rows can drift freely between uses, and drift that never affects outputs is invisible to tests yet exploitable by a malicious prover crafting alternative witnesses. The audit is simple and brutal: for every column, name the constraint that binds every row; columns that only bind conditionally need a default relation (value carries) or removal. This column census catches more real unsoundness than any amount of positive testing.

mainEntity.name: Should new systems ship lattice-based proofs today?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only where the requirement is explicit (government or long-horizon compliance mandates); otherwise hash-based STARKs offer mature tooling, measured performance, and analyses with longer public review. Lattice proof systems are improving quickly -- review annually -- but "post-quantum" in a spec should name assumptions and citations, not vibes, and today the citation depth still favors hashes for production.

mainEntity.name: Does quantum computing break my existing archived proofs?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not retroactively for hash-based systems at adequate margins: an adversary must attack the hash assumptions to forge, and Grover halving at 96-bit leaves ~48-bit margins -- thin but non-trivial; at 128-bit, comfortable. Pairing-based archived proofs are the exposed class: plan re-proving or hybrid re-attestation for those artifacts if their claims must still convince post-quantum.

mainEntity.name: Is "post-quantum" marketing or mathematics in vendor claims?

acceptedAnswer.text: Two implementation notes close the loop for builders. First, hash-agility: name the hash family in every manifest and keep verifier code path-agnostic over families, so a future migration is a parameter rollout with dual-run windows rather than a repository rewrite -- the same versioning discipline the  specifications page  prescribes for protocols applies unchanged to cryptographic primitives. Second, signature hygiene: proof envelopes signed classically today should carry a second, post-quantum signature line where artifact lifetimes exceed a decade; dual signatures cost bytes and buy era-independence, and the bytes are precisely the cheap commodity this cluster keeps trading for properties that age well. Neither note requires new mathematics; both require the record-keeping habit that makes mathematics portable across eras, which is -- after four clusters of evidence -- the single most transferable skill this entire blog teaches.

mainEntity.name: Why not just check random constraints directly without FRI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Direct sampling of constraint values checks the composition polynomial at points, but nothing ties those points to a committed trace the prover cannot adapt per query; FRI's commitments plus proximity close that loop. Sampling without commitment structure is asking the witness to grade itself -- the gap between an audit and a self-report, which is the gap this entire cluster exists to make technical.

mainEntity.name: Does RS structure limit which fields I can use?

acceptedAnswer.text: It requires domains of smooth size (roots of unity) for efficient evaluation and folding, which is why STARK fields are chosen with two-adic structure -- the Goldilocks family's popularity is partly an FFT story. Field selection therefore couples arithmetic speed, security bits, and RS availability; the manifest records the outcome of that coupling, and the field Q&A remains the operational reference for changing it safely.

mainEntity.name: How does list-decoding relevance show up practically?

acceptedAnswer.text: Beyond unique-decoding radius, proximity tests enter list-decoding territory where several close polynomials exist; soundness analyses account for this via careful error bounds per fold, which is why published parameter solvers look conservative versus back-of-envelope unique-distance math. Practically: trust the solver, publish its derivation, and treat hand-tuned "improvements" to query counts as soundness changes -- because that is exactly what they are.

mainEntity.name: Can a proof verify today and fail tomorrow with nothing changed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only if something actually changed: a dependency bump altering field defaults, a rebuilt verifier binary with different feature flags, or clock-free nondeterminism creeping into the prover. Parameter manifests make such changes visible; if the manifests match and bytes match, a previously valid STARK proof remains valid -- the math does not age.

mainEntity.name: Should the verifier return different errors per cause?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, internally -- named errors drive the drift matrix and fast triage. Externally, return one generic code (400/422) with a correlation ID: detailed rejection reasons can leak constraint structure you may not want public, and the correlation ID maps to the internal named error in your logs.

mainEntity.name: Is re-proving on the verifier side ever a legitimate check?

acceptedAnswer.text: As a debugging aid, yes: re-executing the program confirms the claimed outputs. As a substitute for verification, no -- it destroys the point (verifier cost must stay milliseconds, independent of computation size) and silently accepts programs whose proofs you never actually checked.

mainEntity.name: My constraints pass but the prover still rejects -- where next?

acceptedAnswer.text: Leave semantics and check geometry: boundary assertions (first/last row pins), auxiliary column initialization (permutation products must start at identity), and padding length versus declared trace size. These live outside transition evaluation and are the usual home of "constraints green, proof red" -- the parameter half of the drift matrix in the verification-failure Q&A covers the remaining cases.

mainEntity.name: Can I get the prover to print violating rows directly?

acceptedAnswer.text: In debug builds, yes -- wrap constraint evaluation with a recorder as shown above; never in release, since the recording closure costs more than proving at scale. Keep the recorder behind a feature flag with a test asserting the flag changes nothing mathematically (same proofs with flag on), so debuggability never becomes a soundness variable.

mainEntity.name: How do I debug violations that appear only at large trace lengths?

acceptedAnswer.text: Length-dependent deviations are almost always padding or boundary interactions: reproduce at the smallest power-of-two above the failure threshold with synthetic inputs, then shrink inputs until the deviation vanishes -- the last reproducing size brackets the padding boundary. If the bracket is empty, suspect degree-related composition overflow at scale and re-check field size against constraint degree times trace length, the arithmetic the security-parameter manifest exists to keep honest.

mainEntity.name: Will STARK proofs get smaller over time?

acceptedAnswer.text: Incrementally, yes: better folding schedules, base-field FRI variants, and aggregation research shave tens of percent across years. Order-of-magnitude shrinkage would change the proof system's trust or security story, so expect convergence toward "small enough for off-chain everywhere, wrapped for on-chain", not parity with pairing-based bytes.

mainEntity.name: Does compression help (gzip the proof)?

acceptedAnswer.text: Barely: proof bytes are hashes and field elements, already high-entropy; gzip typically saves under 5%. If a channel demands smaller, the honest tools are batching and recursion -- or storing the proof once content-addressed and sending the 32-byte hash plus a retrieval hint, which is what PRF-1 relays do by design.

mainEntity.name: Is 100 KB acceptable for mobile clients?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually yes on modern networks (one image tile costs more), and verification's millisecond CPU cost matters more for battery than the transfer. For constrained IoT, the pattern is delegate: a gateway verifies and returns a signed attestation, or the device runs a minimal verifier like tiny-verify over a locally cached proof -- both keep mobile cost near zero without shrinking the proof itself.

mainEntity.name: Does "no trusted setup" mean no parameters at all?

acceptedAnswer.text: No: public parameters remain -- field choice, security bits, grinding factor, query counts -- but they are public configuration, verifiable by inspection and asserted in every proof envelope. The phrase bans secret trust, not configuration discipline; confusing the two is how teams ship weak parameters believing the setup-free property covers them.

mainEntity.name: Can a prover cheat the grinding nonce?

acceptedAnswer.text: Grinding raises the cost of finding acceptable transcripts; skipping it weakens soundness by exactly the advertised bits, and verifiers check the nonce against the declared factor. A prover that under-grinds produces proofs honest verifiers reject -- the parameter is enforced at verification, which is the only place enforcement means anything.

mainEntity.name: Is Fiat-Shamir a hidden trust assumption?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is a modeled assumption (random oracle), not a trusted party: no human holds anything, and breaks require attacking the hash's structure, not someone's honesty. That distinction -- trust in mathematics versus trust in process -- is the entire content of "no trusted setup", and it is why the answer to this page's question stays a clean no.

mainEntity.name: Can padding make a short trace look normal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, dangerously: padding fills to power-of-two, so a 3-cycle trace presents as 4,096 rows of idle and proofs "succeed" attesting almost nothing. This is why halt-uniqueness and row-count-floor assertions matter more than length checks -- length lies by design (padding), while halt position tells the truth about where your machine actually stopped thinking.

mainEntity.name: My trace is correct but shorter than my cycle estimate -- bug?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily: estimates often count instructions, while cycles count steps (taken jumps cost one, multi-cycle ops cost their declared count). Reconcile against the ISA's cycle semantics table in the  ZKVM-ISA spec ; a trace shorter than instruction count, however, is always a bug, since every instruction costs at least one cycle by construction.

mainEntity.name: Should the executor or the AIR catch these failures?

acceptedAnswer.text: The executor, always: trace-layer failures are specification failures (wrong machine), while AIR failures are legality failures (right machine, illegal step). Catching machine bugs at the AIR costs you prover runs and ambiguous deviations; catching them at execution costs microseconds and names the cycle. The boundary is the same as the one between "the program is wrong" and "the proof is wrong" -- and every hour spent enforcing it early saves three during incident review.

acceptedAnswer.text: For most experienced engineers, three to six weeks of daily use on one real project. mainEntity.name: Should I reach for async immediately in a new service?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Start synchronous with threads until measurement shows you are waiting-dominated (many concurrent idle connections, high fan-out IO). Premature async costs you blocking-call discipline, cancellation design, and debuggability; retrofitting to tokio later is mechanical, while debugging a runtime you did not need is not.

mainEntity.name: When is cloning actually the right answer?

acceptedAnswer.text: When the clone is cheap (Arc, small Copy structs), rare (setup paths, error paths), or buys you a shorter lock scope or a simpler ownership graph. The sin is not cloning; it is cloning in a hot loop without measurement. Clone deliberately, comment why, and let the quarterly clone-audit keep you honest.

mainEntity.name: When should a handler spawn a background task?

acceptedAnswer.text: When the work outlives the request's usefulness: proof generation, report rendering, webhook fan-out. Return an accepted status plus a job id immediately, run the work in a tokio task owned by state (not by the request), and expose status via a job endpoint. Spawning without an owner is how orphan tasks survive shutdown and double-execute after restarts.

mainEntity.name: Is axum's default 2 MB body limit enough?

acceptedAnswer.text: For JSON APIs, yes -- raise it deliberately with DefaultBodyLimit per route when you must accept uploads, and pair any raise with validation and a streaming parser. A global raise to "fix one route" silently turns every endpoint into a memory-exhaustion surface; scoped limits keep the blast radius where you intended it.

mainEntity.name: How do I version an axum API without route chaos?

acceptedAnswer.text: Prefix routers ( /v1 ,  /v2 ) built from shared handler modules, and deprecate by removal only after a logged-usage window: your trace layer already records which clients hit which prefix. Header-based versioning saves URLs but splits behavior invisibly; visible prefixes keep the deprecation conversation honest and the logs readable.

mainEntity.name: How many tasks should one runtime run?

acceptedAnswer.text: As many as your waiting work requires -- tens of thousands is ordinary -- because tasks are cheap until they compute. The real budget is worker-thread saturation: monitor it, and when compute creeps in, move it to spawn_blocking or a dedicated blocking pool rather than shrinking task counts. Task count limits treat the symptom; saturation metrics treat the cause.

mainEntity.name: Is async worth it below ~100 concurrent connections?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually not: threaded-per-connection code is simpler to debug and fast enough at that scale, and retrofitting to async later is mechanical. Adopt async when concurrency is waiting-dominated and large, or when a dependency (an async-only client library) drags you in anyway -- then adopt it fully, with the lint set and shutdown test from day one.

mainEntity.name: Why does my async code use more CPU than the threaded version?

acceptedAnswer.text: Typically poll churn: futures that wake immediately in a loop (busy-wait disguises), excessive tiny tasks spawning per item, or a misused  yield_now . tokio-console's poll-count column exposes it in seconds; the fix is batching work per poll and coalescing wakes. Async efficiency is a scheduling discipline, not a free gift from the keyword.

mainEntity.name: How much space do snapshots really cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: Zero at creation, then churn-proportional: a dataset changing 1% daily costs ~1% of dataset size per daily snapshot until retention prunes it. mainEntity.name: Is RAID-Z1 acceptable for backups pools?

For the only pool holding irreplaceable data, RAID-Z2 or mirrors-plus-offsite is the honest minimum; the topology question is really "how many independent copies exist at every moment", and pools are one answer among several, never the whole answer.

mainEntity.name: Should I encrypt the pool?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes for laptops and any pool whose disks might leave your control (RMA, resale, theft); optional for stationary arrays where the threat model says disks die at home. acceptedAnswer.text: No -- they answer different questions.  restic check  (and  --read-data ) verifies repository structures and pack integrity; a restore verifies that your files, paths, permissions, and retention actually produce usable data on a different host. acceptedAnswer.text: As long as your RTO promises, plus 20% margin -- and if the drill exceeds that, the finding is architectural (faster target, parallel streams, narrower retention) rather than procedural. mainEntity.name: Should drills restore to production or scratch space?

acceptedAnswer.text: Scratch, always, except in a real incident: drills must never mutate production state or compete with production IO. mainEntity.name: Does PersistentKeepalone fix double NAT by itself?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Keepalives keep a pinhole warm toward the configured Endpoint; when both ends are behind symmetric NAT, each keepalive warms a hole the other side's packets still cannot use, because source ports differ per destination. Keepalives fix cone-NAT roaming and idle-timeout cases; double NAT needs an anchor, a relay, or a geometry change as listed above.

mainEntity.name: Can two CGNAT peers connect over IPv4 at all?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only with help: a relay node with a public address (the hub pattern), or hole-punching coordination protocols that WireGuard deliberately does not implement. Accept the relay: one extra hop through your own VPS preserves the mesh's security properties while restoring reachability, and the latency cost for home traffic is milliseconds nobody feels.

mainEntity.name: Is UDP blocking by the ISP a real possibility?

acceptedAnswer.text: Occasionally, especially on mobile-carrier CGNAT and some satellite links that shape or drop long UDP flows. Test by moving the WireGuard port to 443/UDP or tunneling over TCP as a diagnostic only; if that "fixes" it, you have your answer and a decision to make -- permanent TCP tunneling costs performance, so most operators switch that peer to a relay path instead.

mainEntity.name: What breaks first when my ISP changes something?

mainEntity.name: Do SSDs or HDDs survive power loss better?

acceptedAnswer.text: Modern SSDs with power-loss protection capacitors (enterprise and quality consumer NVMe) flush caches reliably; cheap DRAM-less SSDs historically had firmware-level loss bugs, now rare but not mythical. HDDs park heads on power-loss detection using rotational energy -- mechanically elegant and generally safe. mainEntity.name: Is a generator worth it for a homelab?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only where multi-day outages are climatologically normal and your services are genuinely load-bearing (medical, remote-work primary income). For most homes, clean-stop-plus-wake beats generator complexity and fuel logistics; the middle path is a second, larger UPS rotated for battery health, buying an hour of ride-out for the services you flagged battery-critical in the power policy.

mainEntity.name: What about brown-outs and surges specifically?

acceptedAnswer.text: Brown-outs (sustained low voltage) stress PSUs and trip UPSes into battery repeatedly -- a line-interactive UPS with AVR corrects most without battery cycling, extending battery life materially. Surges are handled upstream: a whole-home surge device at the panel plus point-of-use protection for the rack, replaced after any major strike event (their sacrifice is consumable). mainEntity.name: Do guardrail models or classifiers replace gates?

acceptedAnswer.text: They complement, never replace: classifiers detect injection attempts with useful but imperfect accuracy, while gates enforce capability boundaries deterministically. Use classifiers to raise approval thresholds on suspicious sessions (adaptive friction), and gates to make the worst case bounded regardless of classifier verdicts. A classifier-only design bets the estate on a model's mood; a gate-only design misses context -- together they price risk where it belongs.

mainEntity.name: How do I secure agents that must browse the web?

acceptedAnswer.text: Treat fetched content as hostile input by construction: render-free fetchers (text extraction only), egress scoped to allowlisted domains where possible, and zero write-capabilities in the same session as unbounded browsing -- the classic exfiltration channel is a read-capable agent that also holds write or network grants. Split sessions: a reader session summarizes untrusted pages into a sanitized brief; a writer session acts on the brief with gates. Two principals, one workflow, no single session holding both halves of the exfiltration primitive.

mainEntity.name: What is the first gate to add to an existing ungated agent?

acceptedAnswer.text: Network egress deny plus filesystem read-only, granted upward per demonstrated need -- it collapses the exfiltration and destruction classes immediately while leaving most legitimate workflows merely inconvenienced (approvals for the exceptions). Measure the approval queue for a week: it is both your usability budget and your attack-log sample, and it hands you the empirical basis for every subsequent grant, which is how policies grow from evidence instead of anxiety.

mainEntity.name: Should agents be allowed to write their own tools?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only into a sandboxed executor class with its own gate tier, resource ceilings, and egress-deny, and only with generated-code review before promotion to registered tools -- the promotion path is a human approval by design. Agent-authored tools that skip promotion live and die inside the session sandbox; the boundary between "session scratch" and "registered capability" is the load-bearing wall, and walls need doors with locks, not suggestions.

mainEntity.name: How do I handle tools that are reads with hidden writes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Reclassify them: caching layers that persist, analytics calls that phone home, "get" endpoints with rate-state side effects -- audit by running them under strace/network watch at onboarding and file by observed behavior, not by documentation. Tools whose hidden writes cannot be removed get wrapper implementations that make the writes explicit and gated; a wrapper that names the side effect converts a trap into a line item, which is the entire job of this discipline.

mainEntity.name: Is human approval fatigue a real risk?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, and it is the taxonomy's feedback signal: approval queues with >90% rubber-stamp rates mean the class is over-gated (move down a tier with logging) or under-specified (split the class). Measure stamp-rates per class monthly; the goal is approvals that humans read because they occasionally refuse, and classes where refusal never happens are classes whose gate should be a budget instead -- fatigue is not a human failure, it is a taxonomy error wearing human clothing.

mainEntity.name: How large before leaving a single box?

acceptedAnswer.text: Single-box comfortable ceiling: ~5M int8-quantized 768-dim vectors with HNSW in 32 GB RAM including headroom, at interactive latencies. Beyond that, shard by tenant or time (both engines support it) before buying clustering complexity -- sharding on a dimension you already filter by is free partitioning, and free partitioning beats purchased orchestration every time the filter exists.

mainEntity.name: Is disk-based (on-disk HNSW) worth it?

acceptedAnswer.text:
For cold corpora queried occasionally (archives, compliance search), emphatically yes: NVMe-backed indexes cut RAM 5-10x at 2-4x latency, a trade archives happily make. For interactive RAG, keep hot collections resident and archive cold ones to on-disk or to restic shelves with a rehydrate runbook -- tiering vectors like tiering storage is the same discipline at a new altitude, and the runbook row is what makes the cold tier honest. 
 Whichever engine you choose, commission it with the four artifacts every other service in this cluster receives: a runbook page (reindex procedure, restore-from-snapshot steps, embedding-version migration), a heartbeat in monitoring (index lag, query p95, RAM headroom), a backup row naming exactly what is backed up (snapshots or dumps plus the embedding manifest -- backing up vectors without their embedding pin is backing up ciphertext without its key), and a sunset review date for the day corpus growth crosses the single-box ceiling. Engines differ in features; estates differ in whether those four rows exist, and it is the rows, not the engine, that decide whether year two of your retrieval stack reads as operations or as archaeology. Pin the embedding model hash in the same manifest as the index, journal every reindex with its before/after recall on the eval set, and let the manifest plus journal answer the only two questions an audit will ever ask about your retrieval stack: which vectors are these, and what changed them last. 
 When the sunset date arrives and the corpus has outgrown the box, graduation is a config commit plus a reindex window, not a rescue: engines behind one interface, embeddings pinned, backups drilled -- the three properties that turn any future migration into an event with a schedule instead of an incident with a story. Schedules, unlike stories, can be slept through; and a retrieval stack that can migrate in its sleep is the retrieval stack its owners recommend to friends, which is the only endorsement this cluster has ever accepted as evidence.

mainEntity.name: Why is the first token slow but the rest fast?

acceptedAnswer.text: Prompt processing (prefill) is compute-bound over the whole context, while generation is bandwidth-bound per token; long prompts therefore front-load seconds of work. Mitigations: prompt caching for repeated prefixes, chunked prefill on vLLM, and not pasting the novel when a paragraph suffices -- prefill cost is the honest price of context, payable once per unique prefix.

mainEntity.name: Does enabling flash attention change quality?

acceptedAnswer.text: No: it is an exact algorithmic rearrangement (tiling with online softmax), not an approximation -- identical outputs modulo float associativity noise. It changes memory (KV residency drops) and speed (attention kernels fuse), which is why every serving recipe here turns it on; quantized KV, by contrast, is a real approximation and belongs to the quality conversation instead.

mainEntity.name: My tokens/s fluctuate wildly between runs. Why?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually scheduler noise: background indexing, backup windows, or browser tabs competing for bandwidth and cores. Benchmark with the box quiesced and report medians with spreads; if fluctuation persists on an idle box, suspect thermals or power profiles (laptop on battery caps clocks), both of which show in clock logs during the run -- measure the environment before blaming the model, which is innocent more often than its reputation.

mainEntity.name: Does longer context increase local hallucination more than cloud?

acceptedAnswer.text: Context-length sensitivity scales with model class, not hosting: small models degrade faster past their trained context sweet spot, and KV quantization (a local memory-saving habit) adds a second degradation source at long contexts. Keep long-context slots at Q8 KV or above, and chunk-and-retrieve instead of pasting corpora -- the same advice the RAG and VRAM guides give from their own angles, converging because the physics is shared.

mainEntity.name: Can self-consistency sampling fix local hallucination cheaply?

acceptedAnswer.text: Partially and measurably: majority-vote over 5 samples cuts trap-class hallucination roughly in half at 5x compute -- affordable on CPU batches overnight, painful interactively. Use it for offline artifacts (summaries, extractions into records) where latency is free, and spend interactive budget on retrieval and citations instead; sampling tricks are batch economics, not conversation economics.

mainEntity.name: Should user-facing UIs disclose local model use?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, plainly: a one-line model-and-tier indicator per response (name, quant, routing exception if any) matches the citation philosophy and costs nothing. Disclosure converts user calibration from guesswork into habit -- calibrated users report fewer trust incidents and file better feedback, and better feedback is the eval set's most renewable source, closing the loop between honesty and quality in a way no benchmark purchase can.

mainEntity.name: Is self-verification enough for regulated workflows?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is necessary and insufficient: regulators ask for accountability structures (owners, approvals, retention), not just correctness artifacts. Receipts satisfy the integrity column of an audit brilliantly; the authority column still needs named humans at gates and documented delegation chains. Estates that present proofs as compliance substitutes learn the distinction during the audit; estates that present proofs inside a governance story learn nothing, because the audit simply agrees -- which is the entire goal.
